sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Java is a high-level, object-oriented, platform-independent programming language developed by Sun Microsystems (now Oracle) in 1995. It follows the principle of Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA).

sections.heading: Key Characteristics
items: Object-Oriented — everything is modeled as objects and classes.
Platform Independent — compiled to bytecode, runs on any JVM.
Strongly Typed — all variables must have a declared type.
Garbage Collected — automatic memory management.
Multi-threaded — built-in support for concurrent programming.

sections.heading: Android Relevance
sections.content: Java is one of the primary languages for Android development. Android apps compile Java/Kotlin code to bytecode that runs on the Android Runtime (ART).

questions.question: What are the features of Java?
questions.title: What are the features of Java?

sections.heading: Core Features of Java
items: Platform Independent — bytecode runs on any JVM (Write Once, Run Anywhere).
Object-Oriented — supports encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.
Simple — clean syntax, no pointers, automatic memory management.
Secure — no explicit pointer manipulation, bytecode verification, sandboxed execution.
Robust — strong type checking, exception handling, garbage collection.
Multi-threaded — built-in support for concurrent execution.
High Performance — Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler improves runtime speed.
Distributed — supports networking with java.net and RMI.
Dynamic — loads classes at runtime, supports reflection.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Java is platform independent because Java source code is compiled into bytecode (not native machine code), which can run on any machine that has a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) installed.

sections.heading: How It Works
items: Java source code (.java) is compiled by the Java compiler into bytecode (.class files).
Bytecode is not specific to any OS or CPU — it is a universal intermediate format.
The JVM on each platform interprets or JIT-compiles the bytecode into native machine code.
The same .class file runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS without modification.

sections.heading: Slogan
sections.content: Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA) — the bytecode can be executed anywhere a JVM exists.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: JVM stands for Java Virtual Machine. It is an abstract machine that provides the runtime environment in which Java bytecode can be executed.

sections.heading: Responsibilities of JVM
items: Loads .class (bytecode) files via the ClassLoader.
Verifies bytecode for security and correctness.
Executes bytecode using the interpreter or JIT compiler.
Manages memory — heap, stack, method area.
Runs the Garbage Collector to free unused memory.

sections.heading: Android Note
sections.content: Android uses ART (Android Runtime) instead of a standard JVM, but it performs the same fundamental role of running compiled bytecode.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: JDK stands for Java Development Kit. It is a software package that provides everything needed to develop, compile, and run Java applications.

sections.heading: JDK Includes
items: JRE (Java Runtime Environment) — to run Java programs.
Java Compiler (javac) — compiles .java files to .class bytecode.
Development Tools — debugger (jdb), archiver (jar), documentation generator (javadoc).
Java APIs and standard libraries.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.content: JDK is for developers. JRE is for end users who only want to run Java programs.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: JRE stands for Java Runtime Environment. It provides the minimum set of components needed to run a Java application — but not to develop one.

sections.heading: JRE Includes
items: JVM — executes bytecode.
Core Java class libraries — java.lang, java.util, java.io, etc.
Supporting files — property settings, resource files.

sections.heading: JRE Does NOT Include
items: Compiler (javac) — you cannot compile Java code with JRE alone.
Development tools like debugger or javadoc.

questions.question: Difference between JVM, JDK, and JRE?
questions.title: Difference between JVM, JDK, and JRE?

sections.heading: JVM (Java Virtual Machine)
items: Abstract machine that executes Java bytecode.
Handles memory management, garbage collection, and bytecode interpretation.
Platform-specific — different JVM implementations for each OS.

sections.heading: JRE (Java Runtime Environment)
items: JVM + standard libraries.
Used to run Java applications.
Does not include compilation tools.

sections.heading: JDK (Java Development Kit)
items: JRE + compiler (javac) + development tools.
Used to develop and compile Java applications.
Required for Android development.

sections.heading: Relationship
sections.content: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM — JDK is the superset.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Bytecode is the compiled intermediate representation of Java source code. It is not machine code (native code), but a set of instructions understood by the JVM.

sections.heading: Key Points
items: Generated by the Java compiler (javac) from .java source files.
Stored in .class files.
Platform-neutral — the same bytecode runs on any JVM regardless of OS.
JVM interprets or JIT-compiles bytecode into native machine code at runtime.

sections.heading: Android Note
sections.content: Android converts bytecode to DEX (Dalvik Executable) format, which ART then compiles to native code using AOT (Ahead-Of-Time) compilation.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A ClassLoader is a part of the JVM responsible for dynamically loading Java classes into memory at runtime. Classes are loaded only when they are first needed.

sections.heading: Types of ClassLoaders
items: Bootstrap ClassLoader — loads core Java classes (java.lang, java.util, etc.).
Extension ClassLoader — loads classes from the JDK extensions directory.
Application ClassLoader — loads classes from the application's classpath.

sections.heading: Key Points
items: Follows delegation model — child asks parent first before loading.
Prevents loading the same class twice.
In Android, DexClassLoader loads .dex files (used in dynamic feature delivery).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm that organizes software design around objects — instances of classes that combine data (fields) and behavior (methods).

sections.heading: Four Core Pillars of OOP
items: Encapsulation — bundling data and methods together, hiding internal details.
Abstraction — exposing only what is necessary, hiding complexity.
Inheritance — a class can derive properties and behavior from another class.
Polymorphism — the same interface can represent different underlying forms.

sections.heading: Android Example
sections.content: In Android, Activity, Fragment, ViewModel — all are classes following OOP principles. You extend them, override methods, and encapsulate state.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP?
questions.title: What are the four pillars of OOP?

sections.heading: Encapsulation
items: Bundling data (fields) and behavior (methods) inside a class.
Hides internal implementation — access via public methods only.
Example: private fields with getters/setters.

sections.heading: Abstraction
items: Exposing only necessary details, hiding complexity.
Achieved via abstract classes and interfaces.
Example: calling retrofit.getUser() without knowing HTTP internals.

sections.heading: Inheritance
items: A subclass inherits fields and methods from a superclass.
Promotes code reuse.
Example: class MyActivity extends AppCompatActivity.

sections.heading: Polymorphism
items: The same method name behaves differently based on the object.
Compile-time (overloading) and runtime (overriding).
Example: View.onDraw() overridden differently in TextView, ImageView.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A class is a blueprint or template that defines the properties (fields) and behaviors (methods) that its objects will have. It does not occupy memory by itself — only instances (objects) do.

sections.heading: Example
Android Example
sections.content: In Android, Activity, Fragment, ViewModel, and RecyclerView.Adapter are all classes. You create instances of them to build your app.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: An object is an instance of a class. It occupies memory and holds the actual values of the fields defined by the class. Every object has its own state and can perform behaviors defined by its class.

sections.heading: Example
Key Properties of an Object
items: State — current values of its fields.
Behavior — what it can do via its methods.
Identity — unique reference (memory address) that distinguishes it from other objects.

sections.heading: Class
items: A blueprint or template — defines structure and behavior.
Exists only in code, does not occupy heap memory.
Defined once, can create many objects from it.

sections.heading: Object
items: A real instance created from the class.
Occupies heap memory at runtime.
Each object has its own copy of instance fields.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: A constructor is a special method called automatically when an object is created (using new). It is used to initialize the object's state.

sections.heading: Key Rules
items: Has the same name as the class.
Has no return type (not even void).
Called automatically on object creation.
Can be overloaded (multiple constructors with different parameters).

sections.heading: Example
Constructor
items: Same name as the class.
No return type.
Called automatically when object is created.
Used to initialize the object.

sections.heading: Method
items: Any valid name.
Must have a return type (or void).
Called explicitly by the programmer.
Used to perform operations on the object.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: A default constructor is a no-argument constructor automatically provided by the Java compiler if no constructor is explicitly defined in a class.

sections.heading: Key Points
items: Automatically generated if no constructor is written.
Has no parameters.
Initializes fields to default values (0, null, false).
If you define any constructor, the compiler does NOT generate the default one.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: Yes, a constructor can be private. A private constructor prevents external classes from creating instances of the class directly.

sections.heading: Use Cases
items: Singleton pattern — ensures only one instance is created.
Utility classes — prevent instantiation of a class with only static methods.
Factory method pattern — control object creation through static factory methods.

sections.heading: Singleton Example
Introduction
sections.content: this is a reference variable in Java that refers to the current object — the object on which the current method or constructor is being called.

sections.heading: Uses of this
items: Distinguish between instance fields and constructor/method parameters with the same name.
Call another constructor in the same class using this().
Return the current object from a method.
Pass the current object as an argument.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: super is a reference variable in Java that refers to the immediate parent class of the current object. It is used to access parent class members.

sections.heading: Uses of super
items: Access parent class fields that are hidden by child class fields.
Call parent class methods that are overridden in the child.
Call parent class constructor using super() — must be the first statement.

sections.heading: Example
this()
items: Calls another constructor in the same class.
Used for constructor chaining within the same class.
Must be the first statement in a constructor.

sections.heading: super()
items: Calls the constructor of the parent class.
Used to initialize the parent class portion of the object.
Must be the first statement in a constructor.
Automatically added by compiler if not explicitly written.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: Method overloading is defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists (number, type, or order of parameters) in the same class. It is resolved at compile time.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: Also called compile-time polymorphism or static polymorphism.
Return type alone cannot differentiate overloaded methods.
Common in Android: View constructors have multiple overloads.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Method overriding is redefining a method in a subclass that already exists in the parent class, with the same name, same parameters, and same return type. It is resolved at runtime.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: Also called runtime polymorphism or dynamic method dispatch.
Use @Override annotation to catch errors at compile time.
In Android: onCreate(), onResume(), onBindViewHolder() are all overridden.

sections.heading: Method Overloading
items: Same class, same method name, different parameters.
Resolved at compile time (static polymorphism).
Return type can differ.
No inheritance required.

sections.heading: Method Overriding
items: Parent and child class, same method name and parameters.
Resolved at runtime (dynamic polymorphism).
Return type must be same (or covariant).
Requires inheritance.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Dynamic method dispatch is the mechanism by which a call to an overridden method is resolved at runtime rather than compile time. It is the foundation of runtime polymorphism in Java.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: The reference type is Animal, but the object is Dog.
JVM checks the actual object type at runtime to call the correct method.
Enables writing generic code that works with multiple subtypes.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Abstraction is the OOP principle of hiding complex implementation details and exposing only the necessary interface to the user. It focuses on what an object does, not how it does it.

sections.heading: How to Achieve Abstraction in Java
items: Abstract classes — partially abstract, can have both abstract and concrete methods.
Interfaces — fully abstract contract (before Java 8).

sections.heading: Example
Android Example
sections.content: Retrofit abstracts HTTP networking — you define an interface with annotations, and Retrofit handles all the HTTP internals.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Composition is an OOP relationship where a class contains an object of another class as a field. It models a has-a relationship. The contained object's lifecycle is tied to the containing object.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: Strong form of association — component cannot exist without the owner.
Prefer composition over inheritance for better flexibility.
In Android: ViewModel composes a Repository; Repository composes a DataSource.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Aggregation is a weaker form of association where a class contains a reference to another class, but the contained object can exist independently. It models a has-a relationship with independent lifecycles.

sections.heading: Example
Aggregation vs Composition
items: Aggregation — weak relationship; contained object has independent lifecycle.
Composition — strong relationship; contained object dies when container dies.

sections.heading: Association
items: General relationship between two classes.
Neither owns the other.
Example: Teacher and Student — they know each other but exist independently.

sections.heading: Aggregation (Weak has-a)
items: One class contains a reference to another.
Contained object can exist independently.
Example: University has Departments — departments can exist without the university.

sections.heading: Composition (Strong has-a)
items: One class owns another — they share a lifecycle.
Contained object cannot exist without the owner.
Example: Car has an Engine — engine is created and destroyed with the car.

sections.heading: Coupling
items: The degree of dependency between classes or modules.
Low coupling is desirable — classes should know as little as possible about each other.
High coupling makes code hard to maintain, test, and change.
Android example: ViewModel should not depend on Activity — use observers instead.

sections.heading: Cohesion
items: The degree to which a class or module has a single, well-defined responsibility.
High cohesion is desirable — each class should do one thing well.
Low cohesion means a class does too many unrelated things.
Android example: A UserRepository should only handle user data, not UI logic.

sections.heading: Goal
sections.content: Good software design aims for low coupling and high cohesion — components are independent and focused.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: SOLID is an acronym for five object-oriented design principles that promote maintainable, scalable, and testable code.

sections.heading: SOLID Principles
items: S — Single Responsibility Principle: A class should have only one reason to change.
O — Open/Closed Principle: Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification.
L — Liskov Substitution Principle: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
I — Interface Segregation Principle: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use.
D — Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

sections.heading: Android Relevance
sections.content: MVVM architecture naturally follows SOLID — ViewModel has a single responsibility, Repository abstracts data sources, and Dependency Injection (Hilt/Dagger) enforces the Dependency Inversion Principle.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states that a class should have only one reason to change — meaning it should have only one job or responsibility.

sections.heading: Bad Example — Multiple Responsibilities
Good Example — Single Responsibility
Android Example
sections.content: In MVVM: ViewModel handles UI logic only, Repository handles data only, Activity handles only view binding.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP) states that software entities (classes, modules, functions) should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behavior without changing existing code.

sections.heading: Bad Example — Modifying existing class
Good Example — Extend, don't modify
Definition
sections.content: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that objects of a subclass should be substitutable for objects of the superclass without breaking the behavior of the program.

sections.heading: Bad Example — Violating LSP
Good Example — Follows LSP
Android Example
sections.content: Any Fragment subclass should work correctly wherever a Fragment is expected — overriding lifecycle methods should not break the Fragment's contract.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) states that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions.

sections.heading: Bad Example — Tight coupling
Good Example — Depends on abstraction
Android Example
sections.content: Hilt/Dagger injects dependencies — ViewModel depends on a Repository interface, not a concrete class. Makes testing easy by injecting a fake repository.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Access modifiers in Java are keywords that control the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, and fields. They enforce encapsulation by restricting access from outside.

sections.heading: Types of Access Modifiers
items: private — accessible only within the same class.
default (no keyword) — accessible within the same package.
protected — accessible within the same package and subclasses.
public — accessible from anywhere.

questions.question: Difference between private, default, protected, and public?
questions.title: Difference between private, default, protected, and public?

sections.heading: private
items: Accessible only within the same class. Most restrictive.

sections.heading: default (package-private)
items: Accessible within the same package. No keyword needed.

sections.heading: protected
items: Accessible within the same package AND subclasses (even in different packages).

sections.heading: public
items: Accessible from anywhere — any class, any package. Least restrictive.

sections.heading: Access Order (most to least restrictive)
sections.content: private < default < protected < public

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Package-private (also called default access) is the accessibility level when no access modifier is specified. Members with this access are visible to all classes within the same package, but not to classes in other packages.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: More restrictive than protected (which allows subclasses across packages).
Useful for internal helper classes that shouldn't be exposed externally.
In Android, used for classes within a feature module that shouldn't be public API.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The static keyword in Java means that a member (field, method, or block) belongs to the class itself, not to any particular instance. It is shared across all instances.

sections.heading: Uses of static
items: Static fields — one shared copy for all instances.
Static methods — callable without creating an object.
Static blocks — executed once when the class is loaded.
Static nested classes — can be instantiated without an outer class instance.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: The main() method is static because the JVM needs to call it to start the program without creating an instance of the class first. If main() were not static, the JVM would need an object to call it on — but there's no object yet when the program starts.

sections.heading: Signature
sections.code: public static void main(String[] args) { }

sections.heading: Reason
items: static — JVM calls it without creating an object.
public — JVM (external caller) must be able to access it.
void — main() doesn't return anything to the JVM.
String[] args — allows passing command-line arguments.

questions.question: Can static methods access instance variables?
questions.title: Can static methods access instance variables?

sections.heading: Answer
sections.content: No. Static methods cannot directly access instance variables or instance methods. They belong to the class, not to any object, so there is no 'this' reference available inside a static method.

sections.heading: Example
Workaround
items: To access instance variables in a static method, create an instance of the class.

sections.heading: Answer
sections.content: No. Static methods cannot be overridden. They are resolved at compile time based on the reference type, not at runtime based on the object type. This is called method hiding, not overriding.

sections.heading: Example
Why?
sections.content: Overriding requires dynamic dispatch — a runtime mechanism. Static methods are bound at compile time, so there is no dynamic dispatch.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Method hiding occurs when a subclass defines a static method with the same name and signature as a static method in the parent class. The subclass method hides the parent's method rather than overriding it.

sections.heading: Example
Method Hiding vs Overriding
items: Hiding — applies to static methods, resolved at compile time.
Overriding — applies to instance methods, resolved at runtime.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The final keyword in Java restricts modification. It can be applied to variables, methods, and classes.

sections.heading: final variable
items: Value cannot be changed after initialization. Becomes a constant.

sections.code: final int MAX = 100; // Cannot reassign

sections.heading: final method
items: Cannot be overridden by subclasses.

sections.code: final void show() { } // Cannot be overridden

sections.heading: final class
items: Cannot be subclassed (extended). Example: String, Integer.

sections.code: final class Utils { } // Cannot be extended

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The transient keyword in Java marks a field so that it is excluded from serialization. When an object is serialized, transient fields are not written to the byte stream and will have their default values when deserialized.

sections.heading: Example
Use Cases
items: Sensitive data (passwords, tokens) that should not be persisted.
Computed fields that can be recalculated on deserialization.
Non-serializable fields like database connections or threads.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The native keyword in Java declares a method whose implementation is written in native code (C or C++) using the Java Native Interface (JNI). The method body is not written in Java.

sections.heading: Example
Android Use Case
items: Android NDK — writing performance-critical code in C/C++ and calling it from Java/Kotlin.
Used in audio processing, image manipulation, and cryptography for performance gains.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: strictfp is a Java keyword that restricts floating-point calculations to comply with IEEE 754 standards, ensuring consistent results across different platforms and hardware.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: Can be applied to a class, interface, or method.
Ensures portability of floating-point arithmetic.
Rarely used in Android but appears in scientific or financial computation apps.
Since Java 17, all floating-point operations are strictfp by default.

questions.question: How is String implemented in Java?
questions.title: How is String implemented in Java?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: In Java, String is a class (not a primitive) implemented internally as a final char array (before Java 9) or a byte array with an encoding flag (from Java 9+).

sections.heading: Key Implementation Details
items: String is final — cannot be subclassed.
Internally stores characters as private final byte[] value (Java 9+).
Immutable — once created, the content cannot change.
String Pool — string literals are stored in a pool to reuse objects.
hashCode is cached after first computation for performance.

sections.heading: String Pool Example
sections.code:
String a = "hello"; // stored in String Pool
String b = "hello"; // reuses same pool object
System.out.println(a == b); // true — same reference

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: String is immutable in Java — once a String object is created, its content cannot be changed. Any operation that seems to modify a String actually creates a new String object.

sections.heading: Reasons for Immutability
items: Security — Strings are used for class names, URLs, file paths. Mutability could be exploited.
String Pool — immutable strings can be safely cached and shared. Multiple references can point to the same object.
Thread Safety — immutable objects are inherently thread-safe; no synchronization needed.
HashCode Caching — the hash is computed once and cached, since the value never changes.

sections.heading: Android Relevance
sections.content: In Android, passing Strings via Intents or as keys in Maps is safe because they cannot be accidentally modified by another thread.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Immutability means that an object's state cannot be changed after it is created. Once constructed, all its fields remain constant for its lifetime.

sections.heading: Benefits of Immutability
items: Thread safety — no synchronization needed; multiple threads can read safely.
Predictability — state won't change unexpectedly.
Safe to share — can be passed around without defensive copying.
Cacheable — results can be cached since the object never changes.

sections.heading: Examples in Java
items: String, Integer, Long, Double, LocalDate — all immutable classes.

questions.question: How do you create immutable class?
questions.title: How do you create immutable class?

sections.heading: Rules to Create an Immutable Class
items: Declare the class as final — prevents subclassing.
Make all fields private and final — prevents direct access and reassignment.
No setter methods — fields can only be set via constructor.
Initialize all fields in the constructor.
Deep copy mutable fields (like arrays or lists) in constructor and getters.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: The String Pool (also called String Intern Pool) is a special area in the JVM's heap memory that stores unique String literals. When a String literal is created, Java first checks the pool — if an equal string exists, it reuses that object instead of creating a new one.

sections.heading: Example
sections.code:
String a = "hello"; // Added to pool
String b = "hello"; // Reuses pool object
String c = new String("hello"); // Created on heap, NOT in pool

System.out.println(a == b); // true — same pool reference
System.out.println(a == c); // false — different object

sections.heading: Key Points
items: Reduces memory usage by avoiding duplicate String objects.
Only works with string literals — new String() bypasses the pool.
Use String.intern() to manually add a string to the pool.

questions.question: Difference between string literal and new String()?
questions.title: Difference between string literal and new String()?

sections.heading: String Literal
items: Stored in the String Pool.
If the same value already exists in the pool, the same reference is returned.
Memory efficient — no duplicate objects.

sections.heading: new String()
items: Always creates a new object on the heap.
Bypasses the String Pool.
Uses more memory — even if an equal string exists.

sections.heading: Example
sections.code:
String a = "hello";          // Pool
String b = "hello";          // Same pool reference
String c = new String("hello"); // New heap object

a == b  // true
a == c  // false
a.equals(c) // true

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: String interning is the process of storing only one copy of each unique string value in the String Pool. The intern() method returns the canonical representation of the string from the pool.

sections.heading: Example
sections.code:
String a = new String("hello"); // heap object, not in pool
String b = a.intern();           // Adds to pool or returns existing
String c = "hello";              // pool reference

System.out.println(b == c); // true — both reference pool

sections.heading: Use Case
items: Useful when you have many duplicate strings and want to save memory.
Allows == comparison after interning instead of .equals().
Overuse can cause the pool to grow too large in older JVMs.

questions.question: Difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?
questions.title: Difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?

sections.heading: String
items: Immutable — modifications create a new object.
Thread-safe by nature.
Stored in String Pool.

sections.heading: StringBuilder
items: Mutable — modifications happen in-place.
NOT thread-safe.
Faster than StringBuffer.
Use for single-threaded string building.

sections.heading: StringBuffer
items: Mutable — modifications happen in-place.
Thread-safe — methods are synchronized.
Slower than StringBuilder due to synchronization.
Use when multiple threads access the same string.

questions.question: Why is StringBuilder faster than StringBuffer?
questions.title: Why is StringBuilder faster than StringBuffer?

sections.heading: Reason
sections.content: StringBuilder is faster than StringBuffer because StringBuilder is not synchronized — it has no thread-safety overhead. StringBuffer uses synchronized methods, which acquire and release locks on every operation, making it slower.

sections.heading: Key Difference
items: StringBuilder — no synchronization, single-threaded use.
StringBuffer — synchronized, thread-safe, slower.

sections.heading: Recommendation
sections.content: Use StringBuilder in most Android scenarios (single-threaded UI or background work). Only use StringBuffer if multiple threads modify the same string object simultaneously.

questions.question: Difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
questions.title: Difference between shallow copy and deep copy?

sections.heading: Shallow Copy
items: Copies the object and its field values.
For reference fields — copies the reference, not the actual object.
Original and copy share the same nested objects.
Changes to nested objects in one affect the other.

sections.heading: Deep Copy
items: Copies the object and recursively copies all referenced objects.
Original and copy are completely independent.
Changes in one do not affect the other.

sections.heading: Example

questions.question: List all primitive data types in Java.
questions.title: List all primitive data types in Java.

sections.heading: Java Primitive Types
items: byte — 8-bit signed integer. Range: -128 to 127.
short — 16-bit signed integer. Range: -32,768 to 32,767.
int — 32-bit signed integer. Default integer type.
long — 64-bit signed integer. Use L suffix (e.g., 100L).
float — 32-bit single-precision decimal. Use f suffix (e.g., 3.14f).
double — 64-bit double-precision decimal. Default decimal type.
char — 16-bit Unicode character. Stores a single character.
boolean — true or false.

sections.heading: Note
sections.content: Primitives are stored on the stack (when local variables) and are not objects. Each has a corresponding wrapper class (Integer, Long, Double, etc.).

questions.question: Difference between primitive and wrapper classes?
questions.title: Difference between primitive and wrapper classes?

sections.heading: Primitive Types
items: Stored directly on the stack.
Not objects — no methods.
More memory efficient and faster.
Cannot be null.
Example: int, double, boolean.

sections.heading: Wrapper Classes
items: Objects stored on the heap.
Have methods (parseInt, compareTo, etc.).
Can be null.
Required for generics (List<Integer>, not List<int>).
Example: Integer, Double, Boolean.

sections.heading: Autoboxing
sections.content: Java automatically converts between primitives and wrappers when needed (autoboxing/unboxing).

sections.heading: int
items: Primitive type — not an object.
Stored on the stack.
Cannot be null.
No methods.
Faster and uses less memory.

sections.heading: Integer
items: Wrapper class — an object.
Stored on the heap.
Can be null.
Has utility methods: Integer.parseInt(), Integer.MAX_VALUE, compareTo(), etc.
Required in collections like List<Integer>.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: All primitive wrapper classes in Java are immutable — once created, their value cannot be changed. Operations on them return new objects rather than modifying the existing one.

sections.heading: Immutable Wrapper Classes
items: Integer, Long, Short, Byte, Double, Float, Character, Boolean
All declared as final classes.
Their internal value is stored in a private final field.

sections.heading: Example

questions.question: What is memory management in Java?
questions.title: What is memory management in Java?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Memory management in Java is the process of allocating memory for objects and reclaiming it when they are no longer needed. Java handles this automatically via the Garbage Collector (GC).

sections.heading: Key Memory Areas
items: Stack — stores local variables and method call frames. Fast, automatic cleanup.
Heap — stores all objects. Managed by the Garbage Collector.
Method Area / MetaSpace — stores class metadata, static variables, constants.
String Pool — part of the heap that holds unique string literals.

sections.heading: Android Relevance
sections.content: Android has a limited heap per app. Poor memory management (leaks, large bitmaps, static contexts) can cause OutOfMemoryError or ANR.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Heap memory is the runtime data area in the JVM where all objects and arrays are allocated. It is the main memory pool managed by the Garbage Collector.

sections.heading: Key Characteristics
items: Shared across all threads.
Objects live here until they are garbage collected.
Larger but slower to access than stack.
Subject to OutOfMemoryError if full.
In Android, each app has a limited heap size (configurable in manifest).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Stack memory in Java stores local variables, method parameters, and method call frames. Each thread has its own stack. Memory is automatically allocated when a method is called and freed when it returns.

sections.heading: Key Characteristics
items: Faster than heap — LIFO (Last In, First Out) structure.
Thread-private — each thread has its own stack.
Automatically managed — no GC needed.
Fixed size — StackOverflowError if exceeded (infinite recursion).
Only stores primitives and object references (not actual objects).

sections.heading: Answer
sections.content: Objects in Java are stored in the heap memory. The reference (pointer) to the object is stored on the stack, but the actual object data lives in the heap.

sections.heading: Example
Summary
items: Stack — stores primitive values and object references.
Heap — stores the actual objects.
GC manages heap and reclaims memory when objects have no more references.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A strong reference is the default type of reference in Java. As long as a strong reference to an object exists, the Garbage Collector will not collect it.

sections.heading: Example
Android Risk
items: Holding a strong reference to an Activity or Context in a long-lived object (singleton, static field) causes memory leaks.
Use WeakReference<Activity> when you must hold a reference to a Context.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A WeakReference allows the Garbage Collector to collect the referenced object when no strong references exist, even if the WeakReference still points to it.

sections.heading: Example
Android Use Case
items: Used in Handlers, AsyncTasks, or callbacks to hold Activity references without preventing GC.
Always check if .get() returns null before using the reference.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A SoftReference is a reference type where the Garbage Collector will collect the object only when the JVM is low on memory. Unlike WeakReference, soft-referenced objects are kept as long as there is enough memory.

sections.heading: Example
Android Use Case
items: Memory-sensitive caches like image caches.
Prefer SoftReference over WeakReference when you want to keep objects as long as possible before GC.
Modern recommendation: use LruCache (which manages strong references with size limits) instead of SoftReference for image caching.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A PhantomReference is the weakest type of reference. An object with only a phantom reference is eligible for GC immediately. PhantomReference.get() always returns null — you cannot retrieve the object from it.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Used for cleanup actions before the object is removed from memory.
Works with a ReferenceQueue — when the GC is about to collect the object, it enqueues the phantom reference.
Allows more fine-grained resource cleanup than finalize() (which is deprecated).

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: OutOfMemoryError (OOM) is a JVM error thrown when the JVM cannot allocate enough memory for a new object even after GC has run. It is an Error, not an Exception — it usually means the app is in an unrecoverable state.

sections.heading: Common Causes in Android
items: Loading large Bitmaps without scaling or compression.
Memory leaks accumulating over time (leaked Activities, Contexts).
Holding too many objects in memory at once.
Large collections or caches without size limits.

sections.heading: Prevention
items: Use Glide or Picasso for image loading — they handle sampling automatically.
Avoid storing Activity context in long-lived singletons.
Use LruCache with a defined size limit.
Profile memory with Android Studio Memory Profiler.

questions.question: Difference between stack overflow and heap overflow?
questions.title: Difference between stack overflow and heap overflow?

sections.heading: StackOverflowError
items: Stack memory is exhausted — typically from infinite or very deep recursion.
Each method call adds a frame to the stack; too many frames overflow it.
Error is thrown when the stack limit is exceeded.

sections.heading: StackOverflow Example
sections.code: void recurse() { recurse(); } // Infinite recursion → StackOverflowError

sections.heading: OutOfMemoryError (Heap Overflow)
items: Heap memory is exhausted — too many or too large objects.
GC runs but cannot free enough memory.
Thrown as OutOfMemoryError.

sections.heading: Heap Overflow Example
sections.code:
List<byte[]> list = new ArrayList<>();
while(true) list.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]); // OOM

questions.question: What is finalize() and why is it deprecated?
questions.title: What is finalize() and why is it deprecated?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: finalize() is a method in Object that is called by the Garbage Collector just before an object is destroyed. It was intended for resource cleanup (closing files, releasing connections).

sections.heading: Why It Is Deprecated (Java 9+)
items: Unpredictable — no guarantee when or if finalize() will be called.
Can delay GC — objects with finalizers take longer to be collected.
Can cause memory leaks if finalize() resurrects the object.
Thread safety issues — runs on a GC thread, not the app thread.
Better alternatives exist: try-with-resources and AutoCloseable.

sections.heading: Replacement
sections.content: Use try-with-resources to automatically close resources, or use Cleaner API (Java 9+) for post-GC cleanup.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines how threads interact with memory — specifically, how and when changes made by one thread become visible to other threads.

sections.heading: Key Concepts
items: Main Memory — shared memory where all objects live.
Working Memory (Thread Cache) — each thread has a local copy of variables it is working on.
Visibility — without proper synchronization, a thread's changes may not be visible to other threads.
Happens-Before Relationship — a guarantee that memory writes by one thread are visible to subsequent reads by another thread.

sections.heading: How to Ensure Visibility
items: volatile — ensures a variable is always read from and written to main memory.
synchronized — establishes happens-before between threads.
java.util.concurrent classes (AtomicInteger, ConcurrentHashMap) — built-in thread-safe operations.

questions.question: What happens during object creation in JVM?
questions.title: What happens during object creation in JVM?

sections.heading: Steps During Object Creation
items: 1. Class Loading — JVM loads the class if not already loaded via ClassLoader.
2. Memory Allocation — JVM allocates memory on the heap for the object.
3. Default Initialization — all fields are initialized to default values (0, null, false).
4. Constructor Execution — the constructor body runs, initializing fields with actual values.
5. Reference Assignment — the reference variable on the stack points to the new object on the heap.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: Exception handling is a mechanism to handle runtime errors gracefully, preventing the program from crashing. Java uses try-catch-finally blocks and the throws keyword to manage exceptions.

sections.heading: Basic Structure
Benefits
items: Separates error-handling code from normal logic.
Allows recovery from errors.
Provides detailed error information.
In Android: prevents app crashes from network errors, null values, etc.

questions.question: Difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
questions.title: Difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?

sections.heading: Checked Exceptions
items: Checked at compile time — must be handled or declared with throws.
Extend Exception (but not RuntimeException).
Examples: IOException, SQLException, FileNotFoundException.
In Android: used for network or file operations.

sections.heading: Unchecked Exceptions
items: Not checked at compile time — no need to declare or catch.
Extend RuntimeException.
Examples: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IllegalArgumentException.
In Android: usually programming errors (null access, bad index).

sections.heading: Error
items: Serious problems that the application cannot recover from.
Extend Throwable → Error.
Examples: OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError.
You should NOT catch Errors — they indicate JVM/system-level failures.

sections.heading: Exception
items: Conditions that the application can handle and recover from.
Extend Throwable → Exception.
Can be checked (IOException) or unchecked (NullPointerException).
Should be handled using try-catch.

sections.heading: Hierarchy
sections.content: Throwable → Error (serious, don't catch) | Throwable → Exception → RuntimeException (unchecked) | Throwable → Exception → others (checked).

sections.heading: try
items: Contains code that may throw an exception.

sections.heading: catch
items: Handles the exception if thrown. Specify the exception type to catch.

sections.heading: finally
items: Always executes — whether or not an exception was thrown. Used for cleanup (closing files, DB connections).

sections.heading: Example
Answer
sections.content: Almost always. The finally block executes after try (and catch if applicable) regardless of whether an exception was thrown or not. However, there are rare cases where finally does NOT execute.

sections.heading: Exceptions where finally does NOT run
items: System.exit() is called inside try or catch.
JVM crashes or is killed (e.g., kill -9 on the process).
An infinite loop or deadlock inside try — finally never gets reached.
Thread is interrupted or killed before reaching finally.

sections.heading: Practical Rule
sections.content: For all practical Android purposes: always assume finally will run. Use it for cleanup that must happen regardless of success or failure.

sections.heading: throw
items: Used inside a method body to explicitly throw an exception.
Throws a specific exception instance.
Followed by an exception object.

sections.heading: throw Example
sections.code: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid input");

sections.heading: throws
items: Used in method signature to declare that the method may throw an exception.
Tells callers they must handle or propagate the exception.
Followed by the exception type(s).

sections.heading: throws Example
Introduction
sections.content: A custom exception is a user-defined exception class that extends Exception or RuntimeException. It allows you to create meaningful, domain-specific exceptions for your application.

sections.heading: Example
Android Use Case
items: API error responses — throw ApiException with error code.
Repository layer — throw DatabaseException on DB errors.
Makes error handling cleaner and more readable.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Exception propagation is the process where an unhandled exception moves up the call stack from the method where it occurred to its caller, and then to the caller's caller, until it is caught or reaches the JVM (which then terminates the thread).

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: Unchecked exceptions propagate automatically without declaring throws.
Checked exceptions must be declared with throws at each level or caught.
In Android: uncaught exceptions in the main thread crash the app.

questions.question: Can overridden methods throw broader exceptions?
questions.title: Can overridden methods throw broader exceptions?

sections.heading: Answer
sections.content: No. Overridden methods cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions than the parent method. They can throw narrower exceptions, fewer exceptions, or unchecked exceptions.

sections.heading: Example
Why?
sections.content: Callers rely on the parent's contract. If a child could throw broader exceptions, it would break polymorphism — callers who catch IOException would be surprised by unexpected exceptions.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Try-with-resources (introduced in Java 7) automatically closes resources (like streams, connections) after the try block completes. Resources must implement AutoCloseable or Closeable.

sections.heading: Example
Benefits
items: Less boilerplate — no need for manual finally block to close resources.
Safer — always closes even if an exception occurs.
Multiple resources can be declared: try (A a = ...; B b = ...) { }

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. Multiple threads can run concurrently within the same process, sharing memory but having their own stack and execution state.

sections.heading: Key Points
items: Threads share heap memory — can access the same objects.
Each thread has its own stack — local variables are thread-private.
Java Main Thread — starts when the program begins.
Android Main Thread (UI Thread) — handles all UI operations. Blocking it causes ANR.

sections.heading: Creating a Thread
sections.code:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Running in thread"));
t.start();

sections.heading: Process
items: An independent program in execution with its own memory space.
Heavyweight — creating a process is resource-intensive.
Processes don't share memory directly (use IPC to communicate).
In Android: each app runs in its own process.

sections.heading: Thread
items: A lightweight unit of execution within a process.
Threads share the same heap memory.
Cheaper to create than a process.
In Android: multiple threads run in one app process (main, background threads).

questions.question: Ways to create thread in Java?
questions.title: Ways to create thread in Java?

sections.heading: 1. Extending Thread class
items: Override run() method and call start().

sections.heading: 2. Implementing Runnable interface
items: Preferred — allows extending other classes.

sections.code:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Running"));
t.start();

sections.heading: 3. Using Callable + ExecutorService
items: Returns a result. Used with Future.

questions.question: Difference between extending Thread and implementing Runnable?
questions.title: Difference between extending Thread and implementing Runnable?

sections.heading: Extending Thread
items: Your class IS-A Thread.
Cannot extend any other class (Java single inheritance).
Tightly couples your task with thread management.
Less flexible.

sections.heading: Implementing Runnable
items: Your class HAS-A task (Runnable) — separate task from thread.
Can still extend another class.
More flexible — the same Runnable can be submitted to an Executor or wrapped in a Thread.
Preferred approach in modern Java and Android.

sections.heading: Recommendation
sections.content: Always prefer Runnable (or Callable) — it separates the task definition from thread management and is compatible with ExecutorService.

sections.heading: Callable
items: Like Runnable, but its call() method can return a result and throw checked exceptions.
Submitted to ExecutorService.

sections.heading: Future
items: Represents the result of an asynchronous computation.
Methods: get() (blocks and retrieves result), isDone(), cancel().
future.get() blocks until the Callable finishes.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: Synchronization is the mechanism that ensures that only one thread can execute a critical section of code at a time, preventing race conditions and ensuring data consistency.

sections.heading: Synchronized Method
sections.code: synchronized void increment() { counter++; }

sections.heading: Synchronized Block
sections.code: synchronized(this) { counter++; } // More granular control

sections.heading: How It Works
items: Uses an intrinsic lock (monitor) on the object.
Only one thread can hold the lock at a time.
Other threads wait until the lock is released.
In Android: used when multiple threads write to shared state (e.g., shared preferences, caches).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access and modify shared data concurrently, and the final result depends on the unpredictable order of thread execution.

sections.heading: Example
Prevention
items: Use synchronized blocks or methods.
Use AtomicInteger or other java.util.concurrent.atomic classes.
Use ReentrantLock for fine-grained control.
Use thread-safe data structures (ConcurrentHashMap).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Thread starvation occurs when a thread is perpetually denied access to the CPU or shared resources because other threads (usually higher-priority ones) continuously acquire the resources it needs.

sections.heading: Causes
items: Low-priority threads not getting CPU time when high-priority threads dominate.
A thread holding a lock for too long, preventing others from accessing the resource.
Unfair scheduling — some threads always win the lock competition.

sections.heading: Prevention
items: Use fair locking — ReentrantLock(true) creates a fair lock that serves threads in order.
Avoid holding locks for long periods.
Use balanced thread priorities.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The java.util.concurrent.atomic package provides atomic operations on single variables without using synchronization. Operations like increment, compare-and-set are performed atomically using hardware-level CPU instructions (CAS — Compare And Swap).

sections.heading: Common Atomic Classes
items: AtomicInteger — thread-safe integer operations.
AtomicLong — thread-safe long operations.
AtomicBoolean — thread-safe boolean flag.
AtomicReference<T> — thread-safe object reference updates.

sections.heading: Example
sections.code:
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0);
counter.incrementAndGet(); // Thread-safe, no synchronized needed

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: compareAndSet() (CAS — Compare And Swap) is an atomic operation that updates a value only if it currently equals the expected value. It is the foundation of lock-free thread-safe programming.

sections.heading: Signature
sections.code: boolean compareAndSet(expectedValue, newValue)

sections.heading: Example
Use Cases
items: Implementing lock-free data structures.
Safely updating shared counters or flags without synchronized.
Used internally by all java.util.concurrent classes.

questions.question: What is visibility problem in multithreading?
questions.title: What is visibility problem in multithreading?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The visibility problem occurs when one thread modifies a shared variable, but other threads do not see the updated value because they have cached the old value in their local CPU registers or caches.

sections.heading: Example of Visibility Problem
sections.code:
boolean running = true; // Thread 1 sets running = false
// Thread 2 may NEVER see the update if it's cached in a register

sections.heading: Solutions
items: volatile keyword — forces all reads/writes directly to main memory.
synchronized block — establishes happens-before guarantee.
java.util.concurrent classes — built-in visibility guarantees.

sections.heading: Concurrency
items: Multiple tasks making progress — may not run at the exact same time.
Tasks interleave on one or more CPUs.
About managing many things at once (structure).
Example: Android handling UI + network + database on a single-core device.

sections.heading: Parallelism
items: Multiple tasks running at the exact same time on multiple CPUs.
Requires multiple physical cores.
About doing many things at once (execution).
Example: Processing image frames on multiple CPU cores simultaneously.

sections.heading: Key Insight
sections.content: Concurrency is a programming model — parallelism is a hardware capability. Concurrent code can run in parallel on a multi-core device.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Thread safety means that a class, method, or piece of code works correctly when accessed by multiple threads simultaneously, without causing race conditions, data corruption, or unexpected behavior.

sections.heading: Ways to Achieve Thread Safety
items: Synchronization — use synchronized to protect critical sections.
Immutability — immutable objects are inherently thread-safe.
Atomic classes — AtomicInteger, AtomicBoolean for single-variable operations.
Thread-safe collections — ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList.
ThreadLocal — gives each thread its own copy of a variable.

sections.heading: Android Example
sections.content: A Singleton repository accessed from multiple coroutines must be thread-safe — either use synchronized methods or thread-safe data structures.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Serialization is the process of converting a Java object into a byte stream that can be stored to a file, sent over a network, or passed between processes. The object's state is preserved.

sections.heading: Example
Android Note
sections.content: Serializable is slower in Android due to reflection. Parcelable is preferred for passing objects between Activities/Fragments.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Deserialization is the reverse of serialization — it converts a byte stream back into a Java object, restoring its state.

sections.heading: Example
Security Note
items: Deserializing data from untrusted sources can be a security risk.
Always validate the source and consider using safer alternatives like JSON or Protocol Buffers.

sections.heading: Steps
items: Implement the Serializable interface (marker interface — no methods to implement).
Optionally define serialVersionUID to control version compatibility.
Use ObjectOutputStream to serialize and ObjectInputStream to deserialize.
Mark sensitive or non-serializable fields with transient.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: serialVersionUID is a static final long field used to verify that a serialized object is compatible with the class during deserialization. It is a version identifier for the class.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: If not declared, Java auto-generates one based on the class structure.
If the class changes (new fields added) and serialVersionUID changes, deserializing old data throws InvalidClassException.
Best practice: always declare it explicitly and increment when making breaking changes.
In Android: not commonly needed since Parcelable is preferred.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Context in Android holds references to the entire Activity and its view hierarchy. If a Context reference is held beyond the Activity's lifecycle, the Activity cannot be garbage collected — causing a memory leak.

sections.heading: Common Causes
items: Storing Activity context in a static field.
Passing Activity context to a singleton.
Anonymous inner class (Runnable, Thread) holding a reference to the outer Activity.
Non-static inner class Handler referencing the Activity.

sections.heading: Problematic Example
Fix
items: Use getApplicationContext() for long-lived objects.
Use WeakReference<Activity> if you must hold a reference.
Avoid static context references.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: ANR stands for Application Not Responding. It occurs when the Android UI thread is blocked for more than 5 seconds for user input events, or a BroadcastReceiver doesn't finish within 10 seconds.

sections.heading: Common Causes
items: Network calls on the main thread.
Database queries on the main thread.
Long loops or heavy computation on the UI thread.
Deadlocks between threads.
Calling Thread.sleep() or wait() on the main thread.

sections.heading: Prevention
items: Move all heavy work to background threads using Coroutines, Executors, or WorkManager.
Use StrictMode in debug builds to catch accidental main-thread operations.
Profile with Android Studio CPU Profiler.

questions.question: What happens if heavy work runs on main thread?
questions.title: What happens if heavy work runs on main thread?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Android main thread (UI thread) is responsible for rendering UI and handling user interactions. If heavy or long-running work runs on it, it gets blocked.

sections.heading: Consequences
items: UI becomes unresponsive — touch events are not processed.
Frames drop — animations stutter (below 60fps).
ANR dialog shown — if blocked for more than 5 seconds, Android shows the ANR dialog.
Poor user experience — the app feels slow or frozen.

sections.heading: Solution
items: Move heavy work to background threads using Kotlin Coroutines with Dispatchers.IO.
Update UI only on the main thread after background work is done.
Use WorkManager for deferrable background tasks.

questions.question: Explain RecyclerView Adapter using OOP concepts.
questions.title: Explain RecyclerView Adapter using OOP concepts.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: RecyclerView.Adapter is a great example of OOP principles applied in Android.

sections.heading: OOP Principles in RecyclerView Adapter
items: Inheritance — your adapter extends RecyclerView.Adapter<VH>, inheriting its contract.
Abstraction — Adapter is abstract; you must implement onCreateViewHolder(), onBindViewHolder(), getItemCount().
Encapsulation — data list is private; only exposed via adapter methods.
Polymorphism — onBindViewHolder() is overridden to bind your specific data model.
Composition — ViewHolder is a static inner class (composition pattern) that holds references to item views.

sections.heading: Example
Introduction
sections.content: MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel) is an architecture pattern that strongly follows OOP principles.

sections.heading: MVVM and OOP
items: Single Responsibility (SRP) — Model handles data, ViewModel handles UI logic, View handles display only.
Abstraction — Repository abstracts data sources; ViewModel hides data-fetching complexity from View.
Encapsulation — ViewModel exposes only StateFlow/LiveData; internal state is private.
Inheritance — ViewModel extends AndroidViewModel or ViewModel.
Observer pattern — View observes ViewModel's state changes reactively (LiveData, StateFlow).
Dependency Inversion — ViewModel depends on Repository interface, not concrete implementation.

sections.heading: Benefit
sections.content: MVVM produces testable, maintainable code. ViewModel can be unit tested independently since it has no Android UI dependency.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern where an object's dependencies are provided (injected) from outside rather than the object creating them itself. It promotes loose coupling and testability.

sections.heading: Without DI (Tight Coupling)
With DI (Loose Coupling)
DI in Android
items: Manual DI — pass dependencies through constructors.
Hilt (recommended) — Google's DI framework built on Dagger.
Koin — lightweight DI framework for Kotlin.
DI makes swapping implementations easy (e.g., inject a fake repository in tests).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Thread-safe caching ensures that a cache can be read and written by multiple threads simultaneously without data corruption or race conditions.

sections.heading: Options for Thread-Safe Caching
items: synchronized — wrap all cache reads/writes in synchronized blocks.
ConcurrentHashMap — thread-safe map without full locking; allows concurrent reads.
LruCache — Android's built-in LRU cache, thread-safe by default.
Kotlin Mutex (in coroutines) — used when cache is accessed from coroutines.

sections.heading: LruCache Example
Answer
sections.content: No. Constructors cannot be overridden. Overriding is an OOP concept specific to instance methods where a subclass provides a different implementation than the parent. Constructors are not inherited, so they cannot be overridden.

sections.heading: Key Points
items: Constructors have the same name as the class — a Dog class cannot have an Animal() constructor.
Constructors are not inherited by subclasses.
You can overload constructors (multiple constructors with different parameters) in the same class.
A subclass constructor can call the parent constructor using super().

sections.heading: Answer
sections.content: No. Private methods cannot be overridden. They are not visible to subclasses — a subclass can define a method with the same name, but it is a completely new method, not an override.

sections.heading: Example
Why?
sections.content: Overriding requires the method to be visible (at minimum protected or package-private). Private methods are not inherited, so they cannot participate in polymorphism.

sections.heading: Answer
sections.content: Yes. Static methods can be overloaded — you can define multiple static methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class.

sections.heading: Example
Key Distinction
items: Static methods CAN be overloaded (same class, different params).
Static methods CANNOT be overridden (resolved at compile time, not runtime).

questions.question: Why Java is not purely object-oriented?
questions.title: Why Java is not purely object-oriented?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A purely object-oriented language treats everything as an object. Java is not purely OOP because it still supports primitive data types that are not objects.

sections.heading: Reasons Java Is Not Purely OOP
items: Primitive types exist — int, double, boolean, char, etc. are not objects.
Primitives don't have methods and don't extend Object.
Static members belong to the class, not any object.
Wrapper classes (Integer, Double) are added as workarounds for collections.

sections.heading: Contrast
sections.content: Languages like Smalltalk and Ruby are purely OOP — even integers are objects. Kotlin wraps primitives as objects at the language level but compiles to primitives at the JVM level for performance.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Arrays in Java are covariant — if Dog is a subtype of Animal, then Dog[] is also a subtype of Animal[]. This allows an array of a subtype to be assigned to an array of a supertype.

sections.heading: Example
Why Covariant?
items: Designed before generics were added to Java (Java 5).
Allows methods like Arrays.sort() or System.arraycopy() to work on any array type.
Trade-off: covariance can cause ArrayStoreException at runtime if wrong type is inserted.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Generics in Java are invariant — List<Dog> is NOT a subtype of List<Animal>, even though Dog is a subtype of Animal. This prevents type safety issues at compile time.

sections.heading: Example
sections.code:
List<Dog> dogs = new ArrayList<>();
// List<Animal> animals = dogs; // COMPILE ERROR — generics are invariant

sections.heading: Why Invariant?
items: Type safety — prevents inserting a Cat into a List<Dog> at runtime.
Unlike arrays (covariant), generics enforce type rules at compile time.
Use wildcards for flexibility: List<? extends Animal> (covariant read-only) or List<? super Dog> (contravariant write-only).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: ClassCastException is a runtime exception thrown when you attempt to cast an object to a class or interface that it is not an instance of.

sections.heading: Example
sections.code:
Object obj = "Hello";
Integer num = (Integer) obj; // ClassCastException — String cannot be cast to Integer

sections.heading: Prevention
items: Use instanceof check before casting.
In Java 16+: use pattern matching with instanceof — if (obj instanceof Integer i) { ... }
Common Android cause: mismatching View types in adapter's ViewHolder.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: NoClassDefFoundError is a JVM Error thrown when the JVM tries to load a class at runtime that was present at compile time but is missing from the classpath at runtime.

sections.heading: Common Causes
items: A .class file or JAR is missing from the runtime classpath.
The class failed to initialize (static initializer threw an exception).
In Android: a ProGuard or R8 rule stripped a required class during minification.

sections.heading: NoClassDefFoundError vs ClassNotFoundException
items: NoClassDefFoundError — class existed at compile time but missing at runtime.
ClassNotFoundException — class not found when loading dynamically with Class.forName().

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception thrown when you try to load a class dynamically (using Class.forName(), ClassLoader.loadClass()) and the class cannot be found in the classpath.

sections.heading: Example
Android Use Case
items: Used in DexClassLoader for dynamic feature delivery or plugin loading.
Can occur when a class is expected to be loaded dynamically (e.g., JDBC drivers, reflection-based frameworks).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Circular dependency occurs when two or more classes depend on each other, directly or indirectly — creating a cycle. For example: Class A depends on B, and B depends on A.

sections.heading: Example
sections.code:
class A { B b; }
class B { A a; } // A → B → A (circular)

sections.heading: Problems Caused
items: Tight coupling — changing one class forces changes in the other.
Testing difficulty — cannot test one without the other.
Initialization issues — static fields or constructors can cause infinite loops.
In build systems: circular module dependencies can cause build failures.

sections.heading: Solutions
items: Introduce an interface that both classes depend on.
Use dependency injection to break the cycle.
Refactor to extract shared logic into a third class.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Lazy initialization is a design pattern where an object is not created until it is first needed. This avoids unnecessary work and saves resources when the object might not always be used.

sections.heading: Example — Lazy Singleton
Benefits
items: Saves memory — object not created if never needed.
Faster startup — expensive initialization deferred.
In Kotlin: val myObject by lazy { HeavyObject() }

sections.heading: Caution
items: Not thread-safe by default — use double-checked locking or synchronized for multithreaded scenarios.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A race condition happens when two or more threads access shared data concurrently and the program's correctness depends on the relative timing of their execution.

sections.heading: Example
Fix — synchronized
Introduction
sections.content: Thread starvation is a concurrency problem where a thread is perpetually denied access to a resource or CPU time it needs to proceed, because other threads (often higher priority) keep taking the resource.

sections.heading: Example Scenario
Solutions
items: Fair locking — use ReentrantLock(true) to serve threads in FIFO order.
Avoid extreme thread priority differences.
Use fixed thread pools where all tasks get scheduled.
Executor frameworks handle fair scheduling automatically.
